description: We are TRINOVA, a multidisciplinary team participating in the Nairobi local event for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our mission is to build innovative, robust health monitoring software to ensure astronaut safety and well-being on critical space missions.We are actively seeking passionate teammates skilled in Hardware, Software, Coding, Web Development, and Data Analysis who want to push the boundaries of human space exploration. Let's build the future of astronaut health together!
summary:
AURA (Astronaut Understanding, Resilience & Analytics) is a software prototype designed to help astronauts monitor their own health during space missions. It records selected health indicators, presents explainable observations and visually represents available data.

The application provides six main areas: Dashboard, Health Intelligence, Health History, Manual Entry, Mission Simulation and NASA Research Explorer. It supports heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration and mood.

The intended user experience is to enter or review health measurements, compare the latest available measurement with prior history and baseline information, and see understandable non-diagnostic observations. The application includes a separate Mission Simulation workflow using programmed synthetic scenarios.
The NASA Research Explorer uses historical NASA OSDR-575 Inspiration4 serum research. These research values are separate from the astronaut vital-sign analysis workflow and are not treated as live telemetry or clinical reference ranges.
details:
AURA — Astronaut Understanding, Resilience & Analytics

Team: Trinova
Tagline: Beyond monitoring. Towards understanding.

Project Description

1. What does AURA do, and how does it work?

AURA is a software-based astronaut health and wellbeing monitoring prototype designed to help astronauts record, track, and better understand selected health indicators during space missions.

The application focuses on six indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep duration, and mood.

AURA brings together six interconnected application areas:

  • Dashboard: Provides an overview of recorded health information and monitoring activity.
  • Manual Health Entry: Allows users to enter health and wellbeing measurements.
  • Health Intelligence: Uses programmed, explainable rules to compare recent measurements with previous records and available historical or mission-specific baselines, highlighting observable changes.
  • Health History: Allows users to review previously recorded measurements and identify patterns over time.
  • Mission Simulation: Uses programmed synthetic scenarios to demonstrate how the monitoring system behaves under different example conditions.
  • NASA Research Explorer: Provides access to relevant spaceflight biomedical research, including NASA's Open Science Data Repository study OSD-575, which contains blood-serum research from the SpaceX Inspiration4 mission.

The application stores health records locally using SQLite. Its analysis is based on programmed rules rather than an embedded generative-AI medical model. NASA research data are explored separately and are not treated as live astronaut measurements or clinical reference ranges.

2. What benefits does the project have?

AURA aims to make health information easier to record, review, and understand.

Its main benefits include:

  • Centralized monitoring: Brings selected health and wellbeing records together in one application.
  • Historical comparisons: Helps users observe how recorded measurements change over time.
  • Explainable insights: Presents understandable comparisons instead of simply displaying isolated numbers.
  • Mission-context awareness: Supports historical and mission-specific baseline comparisons without intentionally mixing unrelated mission contexts.
  • Demonstration and experimentation: Allows users to explore programmed mission scenarios without requiring physical monitoring hardware.
  • Research accessibility: Connects users with real spaceflight biomedical research through the NASA Research Explorer.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact of AURA is to contribute to the development of more understandable and accessible astronaut health-monitoring software.

During space missions, astronauts operate in environments that can affect physical health, sleep, and psychological wellbeing. AURA explores how software could help organize health information and make changes easier to review.

Our longer-term vision is to develop AURA into a more integrated monitoring platform capable of accepting data from compatible wearable devices and other sensor systems. This could reduce dependence on manual entry and support more continuous monitoring workflows.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did we use?

AURA was developed using a software-focused approach.

Programming language and frameworks:

  • Python — primary programming language.
  • Streamlit — interactive application interface.
  • SQLite — local database for storing health records.

Development tools:

  • Visual Studio Code — development environment
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), particularly study OSD-575.
  • NASA human-spaceflight health and research resources.

The current prototype does not require dedicated medical sensors or wearable hardware. Its initial monitoring workflow uses manual entry and programmed synthetic scenarios, while its architecture is intended to allow future sensor integrations.

5. How is the project creative?

AURA's creativity comes from combining several functions that are often considered separately into one astronaut-focused application.

Instead of functioning only as a digital measurement log, AURA attempts to give recorded measurements context through historical comparisons and understandable observations.

It also combines real spaceflight biomedical research with a separate interactive research-exploration experience and synthetic mission scenarios for demonstrating possible monitoring workflows.

Another important creative decision is the use of explainable, programmed analysis. Rather than presenting an unexplained AI-generated medical conclusion, AURA aims to make its comparisons understandable to the user.

The project also considers future expansion: although the current prototype is software-only, its intended architecture can be extended to support compatible wearable and sensor data sources.

6. What factors did our team consider?

During development, Team Trinova considered several important factors:

  • Astronaut safety: Health information must be presented responsibly, without claiming that the application can diagnose medical conditions or replace professional medical assessment.
  • Usability: The interface should make it straightforward to enter, view, and understand health records.
  • Data accuracy: Measurements, timestamps, units, and historical comparisons must be handled consistently.
  • Mission context: Historical records and baselines should be associated with the correct mission context.
  • Explainability: Users should be able to understand why an observation is displayed.
  • Accessibility: The application should be usable across different devices and screen sizes.
  • Research credibility: NASA research data should be attributed correctly and interpreted within their original scientific context.
  • Scalability: The software should have a pathway towards future wearable and sensor integrations.
  • Privacy: Health-related information requires appropriate protection, especially before any multi-user or operational deployment.
  • Technical feasibility: We prioritized a software prototype that could be developed and demonstrated with the resources available to our team.
